questions.stem: What is the first step of a statistical investigation?
options: Identify an issue and pose a question
Draw graphs of the data collected
Calculate the mean of the results
Choose the sample size of 30 people
questions.explanation: An investigation starts with an issue and a question that data can answer, which then decides who to ask and what to collect. Graphs and summary statistics come after the data are collected.

questions.stem: Which is the best statistical question for an investigation at a school?
options: Do you think that students should work less, yes or no?
How many hours per week do Year 11 students spend on paid work?
How many hours did I spend on paid work last week?
Is paid work good or bad for every student at school?
questions.explanation: A statistical question targets a population and expects answers that vary, which can be collected and summarised. A question about one person has one answer, and good or bad for every student is a matter of opinion rather than data.

questions.stem: A student wants to know how much sleep Year 11 students at her school get on school nights. What is the target population?
options: All Year 11 students at her school
All students at her school
The Year 11 students who answer her survey
All Year 11 students in Australia
questions.explanation: The target population is the whole group the question is about: Year 11 students at her school. The students who answer form the sample, which is chosen from that population.

questions.stem: Which survey question is a leading question?
options: Don't you agree that the canteen's prices are too high?
How would you rate the canteen's prices, from 1 to 5?
How much do you usually spend at the canteen each week?
On how many days each week do you buy from the canteen?
questions.explanation: A leading question pushes the respondent towards a particular answer, here agreement that prices are too high. A rating scale lets people give their own view without being steered.

questions.stem: A survey asks, "Do you exercise regularly?" What is the main problem with this question?
options: It collects numerical data instead of categorical data
Regularly can mean different things to different people
It gives the respondent too many choices to pick from
It asks about two different things in the same question
questions.explanation: The question is ambiguous: one person's regular may be daily and another's monthly, so the answers cannot be compared. A clearer question asks, for example, on how many days in the past week the person exercised for 30 minutes or more.

questions.stem: A survey asks, "How satisfied are you with the bus timetable and the fares?" What is the main problem with this question?
options: It asks about two things, but allows only one answer
It uses a rating scale with too few answer choices
It is a leading question that favours one answer
It asks for personal information that should be private
questions.explanation: Someone might like the timetable but dislike the fares, and one answer cannot show both. Each part needs its own question. The wording does not push the respondent towards an answer, so it is not leading.

questions.stem: A survey asks for hours of homework per week with the choices 0 to 2, 2 to 4, 4 to 6 and 6 or more. What is wrong with the choices?
options: They collect categorical rather than numerical data
They overlap, so 2 and 4 hours fit two categories
There are too many choices for respondents
They leave out students who do no homework
questions.explanation: A student who does exactly 2 or 4 hours could choose either of two categories, so the results are unreliable. Non-overlapping choices such as 0 to less than 2, and 2 to less than 4, fix this. 0 is already included in the first choice.

questions.stem: A survey asks, "How do you usually travel to school?" with the choices car, bus and train. What is the problem with the choices?
options: They include too many forms of transport
They make the question a leading one
They overlap, so a student could pick two
They leave out walking, cycling and other ways
questions.explanation: Students who walk or cycle have no correct choice, so they may skip the question or pick a wrong one. Adding walk, cycle and an other option covers everyone. The three choices do not overlap.

questions.stem: Which survey question best follows the principles of clear language, unambiguous wording and a sensible number of choices?
options: Do you agree that breakfast is the most important meal of the day?
Do you usually eat a healthy breakfast and lunch on school days?
How often do you eat breakfast? (never, sometimes, often, usually, always, mostly)
In the past 7 days, on how many days did you eat breakfast? (0 to 7)
questions.explanation: The first question fixes a time period and asks for a count, so every respondent understands it the same way. The others are leading, ask two things at once, or offer vague, overlapping choices such as often, usually and mostly.

questions.stem: How can a survey best protect the privacy of the people who take part?
options: Publish each person's answers with their name
Ask for full names and addresses on every survey
Share the raw responses with anyone who asks
Keep responses anonymous and store them securely
questions.explanation: Anonymous responses that are stored securely cannot be traced back to individuals, which also encourages honest answers. Collecting names and addresses that the investigation does not need puts privacy at risk.

questions.stem: Which practice is required for a survey to be ethical?
options: Participants are not told the purpose of the survey, to avoid bias
Participants must answer every question before they may leave
Participants are chosen only if they will support the hypothesis
Participants give informed consent and may withdraw at any time
questions.explanation: Ethical data collection means people know what the survey is for, agree to take part and can stop at any time. Choosing only supporters would also bias the results.

questions.stem: A council surveys residents about a new library, but the survey is only available in English. Many residents mainly speak other languages. What is the main problem?
options: The survey will produce numerical data instead of categorical data
The sample becomes a stratified sample rather than a random one
The survey cannot be analysed because the sample is too large
Those residents are likely to be under-represented in the results
questions.explanation: If many residents cannot easily read the survey, their views will be missing, so the results will not reflect the whole community. Offering the survey in community languages makes it responsive to diverse groups.

questions.stem: An interviewer asks shoppers about a new supermarket while wearing the supermarket's uniform. What kind of problem could this cause?
options: A sampling error, because the sample is chosen by systematic sampling
A classification error, because the answers will be numerical data
Bias, because people may give answers they think the interviewer wants
A privacy breach, because the interviewer can see each shopper's face
questions.explanation: Respondents tend to answer politely or favourably when they know who is asking, which biases the results towards the supermarket. A neutral interviewer or an anonymous survey reduces this.

questions.stem: In a simple random sample, which statement is true?
options: Every kth member of an ordered list of the population is selected
Members of the population choose for themselves whether to take part
The population is split into groups and each group is sampled in proportion
Every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
questions.explanation: Random sampling gives every member the same chance of selection, for example by drawing names or using random numbers. Choosing every kth member is systematic sampling, and sampling groups in proportion is stratified sampling.

questions.stem: What is systematic sampling?
options: Choosing members from each subgroup in proportion to its size
Choosing the members who are easiest for the researcher to reach
Choosing every kth member from a list, after a random start
Choosing members who volunteer to answer the survey
questions.explanation: Systematic sampling picks members at a fixed interval, such as every 20th name on a list, starting from a randomly chosen position. Volunteers make a self-selected sample.

questions.stem: A school of 600 students uses systematic sampling to choose 30 students. The first student chosen is number 7 on the list. What is the number of the fourth student chosen?
questions.explanation: The interval is 600 ÷ 30 = 20, so the students chosen are 7, 27, 47, 67, and so on. The fourth is 67. 87 is the fifth, and 47 is the third.

questions.stem: A radio station asks listeners to phone in and vote on a local issue. What type of sample is this?
options: Random
Self-selected
Systematic
Stratified
questions.explanation: The listeners decide for themselves whether to take part, which makes it a self-selected sample. People with strong views are the most likely to call, so it is rarely representative.

questions.stem: A school has 320 students in Year 11 and 480 in Year 12. A stratified sample of 50 students is taken from these two years. How many should come from Year 11?
questions.explanation: Year 11 is 320 ÷ 800 = 40% of the students, and 40% of 50 = 20. 25 splits the sample evenly, which ignores the different sizes of the two groups, and 30 is the Year 12 share.

questions.stem: A club has 600 junior, 525 senior and 375 veteran members. A stratified sample of 60 members is chosen. How many veterans should be in the sample?
questions.explanation: The total is 1500, so veterans make up 375 ÷ 1500 = 25%, and 25% of 60 = 15. 20 shares the sample equally among the three groups, and 24 is the number of juniors.

questions.stem: Why is a self-selected sample often not representative of the population?
options: Every member has the same chance of being chosen for it
The sample is always larger than the whole population
Members are chosen at fixed intervals from a list
People with strong opinions are more likely to take part
questions.explanation: When people choose whether to respond, those who care most, often with strong or extreme views, are over-represented. An equal chance of selection describes a random sample, which avoids this.

questions.stem: A researcher divides a town's adults into age groups, then randomly selects people from each group in proportion to the group's size. Which sampling method is this?
options: Self-selected sampling
Simple random sampling
Stratified sampling
Systematic sampling
questions.explanation: Splitting the population into subgroups and sampling each in proportion is stratified sampling. Selection within each group is random, but the method as a whole is stratified.

questions.stem: To estimate how residents travel to work, a survey is handed out at a train station at 8 am on a weekday. Why is the sample unlikely to be representative?
options: It over-represents people who travel by train
It is a stratified sample, so it overstates every group
The sample was chosen at random, so it is unreliable
Asking at 8 am makes the data numerical, not categorical
questions.explanation: Almost everyone at a station is a train user, so drivers, cyclists and people who work from home are largely missed. The sampling method decides whether a sample represents the population, regardless of how many people answer.

questions.stem: A council uses systematic sampling to survey every 10th house on a street. Every 10th house on the street happens to be a large corner block. What is the problem?
options: The sample may contain only corner blocks, which is biased
Systematic sampling cannot be used for houses on a street
The sample will be too large to give useful information
Every house will have an equal chance of selection instead
questions.explanation: If the list has a repeating pattern that matches the sampling interval, systematic sampling can pick only one type of member. A different starting point, interval or method would avoid sampling only the corner blocks.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of a stratified sample over a simple random sample?
options: It always needs a smaller sample than a random sample
It makes sure each subgroup is represented in proportion
It lets people decide for themselves whether to take part
It needs no list or information about the population
questions.explanation: A simple random sample could, by chance, include too few members of a small group. Stratifying guarantees each group its fair share, but it needs information about the sizes of the groups.

questions.stem: Researchers record people's diets and their heart health over 10 years without changing what anyone eats. What type of study is this, and what is its main limitation?
options: An experiment, which cannot by itself show cause and effect
An observational study, which shows cause and effect directly
An experiment, which uses a self-selected sample of patients
An observational study, which cannot by itself show cause and effect
questions.explanation: The researchers observe without imposing a treatment, so it is an observational study. Other factors, such as exercise, could explain a link between diet and heart health, so it cannot prove that diet is the cause.

questions.stem: A teacher gives her class a new revision app and their test marks rise. She concludes the app caused the improvement. What is the main fault in her conclusion?
options: There was no control group to compare against
The sample was chosen by systematic sampling
Test marks are categorical rather than numerical
The class is too large to give a reliable result
questions.explanation: Marks might have risen anyway, for example because the topic was easier or students studied more. Comparing with a similar class that did not use the app, a control group, is needed to judge the app's effect.

questions.stem: A student surveys 5 friends and concludes that most students at his school of 900 prefer online lessons. What are the main faults?
options: The question was posed to the whole target population
The sample is very small and not randomly chosen
The sample is stratified and the data are numerical
The sample is too large for the size of the school
questions.explanation: Five people cannot reliably represent 900, and friends are likely to share opinions, so the sample is both too small and biased. A larger random sample would be more representative.

questions.stem: A news headline reads "Thefts double at local park!" The number of thefts rose from 2 to 4 in a year. Why is the headline misleading?
options: With such small numbers, a change of 2 makes the rise sound dramatic
Doubling means the number of thefts increased by 200 percent
The number of thefts is categorical data, so it cannot double
A rise from 2 to 4 is an increase of 50 percent, not double
questions.explanation: 4 is indeed double 2, but two extra thefts is a small change that could easily happen by chance. Describing it as doubling, without the actual numbers, misrepresents the data. Doubling is a 100% increase, not 200%.

questions.stem: A survey is posted to 2000 households and only 150 are returned. What is the main fault in using the results to describe all the households?
options: Posting the survey made it a stratified sample
A 7.5% response gives exactly 7.5% of the true answer
Those who replied may differ from the many who did not
The sample was too large for the population surveyed
questions.explanation: With only 7.5% responding, the results may reflect people with more time or stronger views, and the other 92.5% could think differently. This is called non-response bias. The sample was too small in effect, not too large.

questions.stem: A report notes that ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer and claims that eating ice-cream causes drowning. What is the misunderstanding?
options: The data are categorical, so no link can be found
The sample size is too large to show a link
Drownings cause people to buy more ice-cream
Both are linked to a third factor, hot weather
questions.explanation: Hot weather increases both ice-cream sales and swimming, so the two rise together without one causing the other. Reporting a link as cause and effect is a common misrepresentation of data.

questions.stem: Which variable is categorical?
options: Favourite sport
Number of siblings
Height in centimetres
Hours slept last night
questions.explanation: Favourite sport is recorded as a category, such as netball or soccer, not as a number. The others are counted or measured, so they are numerical.

questions.stem: Which variable is numerical and discrete?
options: The number of rooms in a house
The temperature at midday
A person's place of birth
The time taken to run 100 m
questions.explanation: Rooms are counted, so the values are whole numbers with gaps between them: discrete. Temperature and time are measured on a continuous scale, and place of birth is categorical.

questions.stem: Which variable is numerical and continuous?
options: Hours slept last night
Number of phones in a home
Song genre
Goals scored in a match
questions.explanation: Time slept is measured and can take any value in a range, such as 7.25 hours, so it is continuous. Phones and goals are counted, which makes them discrete.

questions.stem: A survey records each person's income bracket: under $50 000, $50 000 to $99 999, or $100 000 and over. How is this variable classified?
options: Numerical and continuous
Numerical and discrete
Categorical and ordinal
Categorical and nominal
questions.explanation: The responses are categories, but they have a natural order from lowest to highest, so the variable is ordinal. Nominal categories, such as car model, have no order. The dollar figures label the brackets rather than recording each income.

questions.stem: How is the variable car model classified?
options: Categorical and ordinal
Numerical and discrete
Numerical and continuous
Categorical and nominal
questions.explanation: Car models are names with no natural order, so the variable is nominal categorical. Ordinal categories, such as fan speed low, medium and high, can be ranked.

questions.stem: A fan's speed can be recorded either as 1, 2 or 3, or as low, medium or high. Which statement is correct?
options: Recorded as 1, 2, 3 it is continuous, because fan speeds can take any value
Recorded as low, medium, high it is numerical, because the speeds can be ranked
Recorded as 1, 2, 3 it can be treated as numerical; as low, medium, high it is ordinal
Recorded either way it is nominal, because the labels can always be changed
questions.explanation: The same information can be numerical or categorical depending on how responses are recorded. As words the speeds are ordered categories, so ordinal; being able to rank them does not make them numerical. The settings are separate values, so they are not continuous.

questions.stem: How is shoe size, recorded in Australian sizes such as 8, 8.5 and 9, classified?
options: Numerical and discrete
Numerical and continuous
Categorical and nominal
Neither numerical nor categorical
questions.explanation: Shoe sizes can only take set values, such as whole and half sizes, with nothing in between, so the variable is discrete numerical. Foot length is continuous, but the size recorded is not.
